analysis.one_liner: Cuts fees, appraisals, and paperwork barriers so homeowners with Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac loans can refinance at low rates.
analysis.headline: The bill to lower refinancing costs for underwater homeowners died in the Senate Banking Committee after a single hearing, with no committee vote and no floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Millions of homeowners owed more on their mortgages than their homes were worth after the housing crash. Many had loans backed by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac and were paying off their mortgages on time, but at interest rates well above the record lows of 2012. This bill would have forced Fannie and Freddie to let those homeowners refinance cheaply: no up-front fees, streamlined appraisals instead of costly full ones, uniform rules so any lender could participate, and a 5% penalty on banks or mortgage insurers that blocked a refinance by refusing to refile a second lien or transfer insurance. It died in committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners who were current on mortgages owned or guaranteed by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac — especially those whose loan balances exceeded their home values. They could have refinanced into lower monthly payments without paying for a full appraisal or up-front lender fees, regardless of how far underwater they were or whether they had a job loss in their history.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Underwater but current homeowners with Fannie/Freddie loans

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have made all borrowers current on their Fannie/Freddie mortgages eligible for streamlined refinancing, and barred the companies from rejecting or charging them more based on loan-to-value, combined loan-to-value, employment status, or income.
It would have prohibited up-front charges to lenders — loan-level price adjustments and similar fees — which are typically passed on to borrowers as higher closing costs.
It would have required streamlined alternative valuation methods instead of full appraisals, with Fannie and Freddie absorbing any manual appraisal costs rather than billing the borrower or lender.

It would have imposed a 5% penalty, applied to the borrower's first-mortgage balance, on a junior lien holder or mortgage insurer whose refusal to resubordinate or transfer coverage blocked the refinance — the two most common third-party roadblocks.

It would have required Fannie and Freddie to notify every borrower with a GSE loan about the program, and to maintain a public website where borrowers could check eligibility, find participating lenders, and calculate potential savings.

It would have required Fannie and Freddie to make their refinancing guidelines consistent, so lenders would not need different rulebooks for each company — a barrier that had limited which lenders participated.

analysis.who_pays: Banks and other holders of junior liens (second mortgages and HELOCs) that faced a 5% penalty if they refused to let a refinance proceed, and private mortgage insurers facing the same penalty for refusing to transfer coverage. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac — and ultimately the taxpayers standing behind them during conservatorship — would bear appraisal costs and the administrative cost of the expanded program, though the bill set a floor on the guarantee fees they charge so fee revenue would not drop.
analysis.who_pays_short: Second-lien holders and mortgage insurers that block refinances

drawbacks.text: The bill set a floor on guarantee fees at no less than their 2012 average and barred the companies from offsetting the fee by lowering other charges, meaning refinancing under the program would not have gotten cheaper through reduced guarantee fees — the fee revenue flowing to the GSEs was protected.

The 5% penalty on junior lien holders and mortgage insurers is a blunt instrument; an honest supporter would acknowledge it forces private financial firms to absorb losses on existing contracts to enable someone else's refinance, and that the exceptions list and FHFA discretion would invite disputes over when the fine applies.
Eligibility was limited to borrowers current on their mortgages, with no more than one late payment in the prior year — so homeowners already in serious distress got no help from this bill.

Because Fannie and Freddie were in federal conservatorship, opponents argued that loosened underwriting and streamlined appraisals shifted additional refinancing risk onto the enterprises and the taxpayers backing them; the bill tried to blunt this by keeping guarantee fees at 2012 levels, but the risk objection was the core argument against it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the targeted group — homeowners current on GSE-backed mortgages who were paying above-market rates — the benefits were concrete and large: lower monthly payments with little paperwork and no appraisal cost, in an economy where consumer spending was a key to recovery. The costs fell on identifiable concentrated interests (second-lien holders, mortgage insurers) and on the GSEs' administrative burden, while the guarantee-fee floor protected the federal backstop from losing fee revenue. The main honest criticism is design, not purpose: the penalty mechanism was aggressive, the guarantee-fee floor limited how cheap the refinance could get, and struggling borrowers already behind on payments were excluded. On balance, the bill directed real savings to ordinary households at the expense of firms that were profiting from blocking them.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2012, referred to the Senate Banking Committee, got one hearing, and then simply sat there — no committee vote, no floor action — until the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Senator Robert Menendez introduced the bill on May 10, 2012, with ten original Senate cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs on the day it was introduced.
The committee held a hearing on the bill on May 24, 2012, printed as S.Hrg. 112-709.
No further action was ever taken: the record shows no markup, no committee vote, no floor debate, and no roll call before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.
All 14 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Second-lien holders and mortgage insurers kept the ability to block refinances, and underwater homeowners kept paying higher rates. No Republican-backed alternative advanced either — the status quo won by default.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Second-lien banks, mortgage insurers, and the status quo

for.name: Sen. Robert Menendez
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited ten original Senate cosponsors.

for.name: Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 14 cosponsors were Democrats.

for.name: President Obama
for.what_they_did: Publicly urged Congress in 2012 to pass legislation expanding refinancing for GSE borrowers, making it a signature item of his economic agenda.

against.name: Sen. Tim Johnson
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Held one hearing on the bill but never scheduled a committee vote, leaving the bill to die in committee.

against.name: Edward DeMarco
against.role: Acting Director, Federal Housing Finance Agency (regulator of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac)
against.what_they_did: Opposed expanding refinancing of GSE loans on the grounds that it would shift costs to the enterprises and the taxpayers supporting them, giving senators a policy rationale to leave the bill alone.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Provided no cosponsors and generally opposed mandatory GSE refinancing expansion as a taxpayer risk.

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a Democrat (14 total) and no Republican signed on; the bill then died in the Democratic-chaired Banking Committee without ever reaching a vote.

industries.industry: Second-lien holders (banks holding second mortgages and HELOCs)
industries.note: The bill fined these firms 5% of the first-mortgage balance if they refused to resubordinate a junior lien, which was a common way a refinance got blocked. Their interest in preserving that veto power ran directly against borrowers trying to lower their payments.

The bill applied the same 5% penalty if a mortgage insurer refused to transfer coverage to the new loan or added fees as a condition. Insurers had an incentive to block refinances to keep premiums on old loans; the bill removed that leverage.

Streamlined rules, no up-front GSE fees, uniform guidelines, and relief from most representations and warranties would have lowered lenders' costs and opened the refinance market to more of them. Their gain came from the same volume that lowered borrowers' payments.

industries.industry: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac (and the taxpayers behind them)
industries.note: The enterprises would have taken on appraisal costs and more refinancing volume under relaxed rules, but the bill locked in guarantee fees at no less than their 2012 average and barred offsetting cuts, protecting the fee income the federal backstop relied on while in conservatorship.
